NCT05918211.what_is_this_study_about: FUEL-2 is testing whether a medicine called udenafil can safely help teens with Fontan circulation exercise better. Teens take either udenafil or a placebo twice a day for 26 weeks. A placebo looks like the study medicine but has no active drug. Neither families nor the study team know which one a teen receives. Exercise tests before and after treatment measure how well the body uses oxygen during exercise.
NCT05918211.who_might_this_be_for: Teens ages 12 through 18 who have had the Fontan procedure may qualify. They must be able to complete exercise testing and meet the study's other health requirements. Some health conditions, medicines, a recent hospital stay for worsening heart failure, or being evaluated or listed for a heart transplant may prevent someone from joining. The study team will review all eligibility requirements.
NCT05918211.why_might_this_matter: Some teens with Fontan circulation have trouble with exercise. This study may help researchers learn whether udenafil improves exercise ability and what side effects it may cause. Researchers will also study blood markers related to liver scarring. Taking part may or may not directly benefit a teen in the study.
NCT05918211.what_should_families_know: The study lasts about six months and includes study medicine and exercise testing. Families should ask how many visits are required, what tests will be done, and what side effects are possible. The study reports that travel costs are covered and families may receive payment for taking part. Families should confirm these details with the study team.

NCT06762964.what_is_this_study_about: This study is testing whether dapagliflozin can improve blood flow in adults who are having problems with their Fontan circulation. Participants are randomly assigned to take either dapagliflozin or a placebo once a day for 12 weeks. Neither participants nor the researchers know which treatment a person receives. Researchers will compare pressure in the veins at rest and during exercise before and after treatment.
NCT06762964.who_might_this_be_for: Adults age 18 or older who have had a Fontan procedure and have shortness of breath may qualify. Participants must also have high pressure in their veins at rest or during exercise, which is measured during the first study visit. Some heart, kidney, or liver problems and certain medicines may prevent someone from joining. People with Type 1 diabetes cannot participate. The study team will review all eligibility requirements.
NCT06762964.why_might_this_matter: High pressure in the veins can contribute to health problems in people with Fontan circulation. Researchers want to learn whether dapagliflozin can lower this pressure and improve how the heart and circulation respond to exercise. The study will also look at exercise ability, blood volume, body composition, and quality of life.
NCT06762964.what_should_families_know: Participants take dapagliflozin or a placebo every day for 12 weeks. Testing is done before and after treatment and includes exercise testing, heart and circulation measurements, body composition scans, and quality-of-life questions. The study also measures blood volume using a small amount of radioactive material. An invasive measurement of pressure in a vein is used during screening, and people whose pressure is not high enough cannot continue into the treatment part of the study. The study plans to enroll 27 people.

NCT05647213.what_is_this_study_about: This Phase 1 study is testing the safety of an experimental treatment made from a participant's own cells. Researchers first collect cells through a small skin biopsy. In the laboratory, these cells are used to create stem cells and then heart cells. About nine months later, participants who have suitable cells and meet the study requirements may receive one dose of the lab-grown heart cells. The main goals are to learn whether this treatment can be given safely to people and whether this type of study is possible to carry out.
NCT05647213.who_might_this_be_for: Adults ages 18 through 40 with single ventricle heart disease and very advanced heart failure may qualify. Participants must have severely decreased heart function and an estimated life expectancy of about 1 to 1.5 years. They must also be waiting for a heart transplant but unlikely to receive one in time, have been denied a transplant for medical reasons, or be using or planning long-term mechanical heart support. The study has many additional health and safety requirements that the study team will review.
NCT05647213.why_might_this_matter: People with end-stage single ventricle heart failure may have very limited treatment options. Researchers are studying whether heart cells made from a person's own cells can be safely given to people with congenital heart disease. Because this is an early Phase 1 study, it is designed mainly to study safety and feasibility, not to prove that the treatment improves heart function or helps people live longer.
NCT05647213.what_should_families_know: Participation begins with a skin biopsy, and making the experimental heart cells takes about nine months. Not everyone who enrolls will receive the cells; participants who do not receive the experimental product are followed as a comparison group. Those who receive the cells need extensive testing, heart-rhythm monitoring, and other safety measures, and must have someone with them around the clock during the first three weeks after treatment. The study includes long-term safety monitoring, including testing for tumor markers, and participants agree to lifelong follow-up. Families should ask the study team for a detailed explanation of how the cells are given, the known and unknown risks, the monitoring required before and after treatment, and what happens if a participant's health changes while the cells are being prepared.

NCT06461676.what_is_this_study_about: This early-stage study is testing VentriGel, a material designed to support heart muscle, in babies with hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS). During the Glenn operation, doctors give eight small injections of VentriGel directly into the right ventricle, the main pumping chamber in children with HLHS. The main goal is to learn whether this treatment is safe and practical. Researchers will also look for early signs that it may improve how well the right ventricle works.
NCT06461676.who_might_this_be_for: Babies under 1 year old with HLHS who are having their Stage II Glenn operation may qualify. Some health problems may prevent a baby from joining, including certain heart rhythm problems, blood-clotting disorders, immune system problems, a history of cancer, or abnormal blood test results. Babies who recently needed mechanical heart support may also not qualify. The study team will review all eligibility requirements.
NCT06461676.why_might_this_matter: In HLHS, the right ventricle has to do the work of pumping blood to the body. Over time, this extra work can lead to problems with heart function. Researchers hope VentriGel may help support the right ventricle, but this has not yet been shown in children with HLHS. This Phase 1 study is mainly designed to learn about safety, not to prove that VentriGel improves heart function.
NCT06461676.what_should_families_know: VentriGel is a gel-like material made from processed pig heart tissue. It is given during the Glenn operation, while the baby is already on the heart-lung bypass machine, through eight small injections into the right ventricle. All babies in this study receive VentriGel; there is no placebo group. Researchers closely watch for safety problems after surgery, including abnormal heart rhythms, bleeding, stroke, and other serious complications. Follow-up testing includes echocardiograms and heart MRI scans for up to 12 months. The study plans to enroll only 12 babies.

NCT04467671.what_is_this_study_about: This study is testing a tissue-engineered vascular graft in people having an extracardiac Fontan operation. The graft is a specially made tube that is used to connect the large vein from the lower body to the arteries going to the lungs. Researchers want to learn how safely the graft works and how it changes over time. Everyone in the study receives the new graft; there is no placebo or comparison group.
NCT04467671.who_might_this_be_for: People with single ventricle heart disease who are preparing for an extracardiac Fontan operation may qualify. Some health problems may prevent someone from joining, including kidney problems, certain blood flow or heart valve problems, or having a pacemaker. The size of graft needed must also fall within the study's range. People who need urgent or emergency surgery cannot participate. The study team will review all eligibility requirements.
NCT04467671.why_might_this_matter: The tube used during an extracardiac Fontan becomes a permanent part of the Fontan circulation. Researchers hope a tissue-engineered graft may be able to grow or change with the body over time. This study will help researchers learn how the graft performs and whether problems such as narrowing, blood clots, infection, or widening of the graft occur.
NCT04467671.what_should_families_know: The study changes the type of graft used during the Fontan operation. Participants must return to Nationwide Children's Hospital for follow-up for at least two years. Follow-up includes exams, echocardiograms, and MRI scans to check the graft and watch how it changes over time. This is a Phase 2 study that plans to enroll 24 participants. Families should ask the study team about the known and unknown risks of the graft, how study follow-up differs from usual Fontan care, and what travel will be required.

NCT02852031.what_is_this_study_about: This study is a large registry that collects information about babies with hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) and related single ventricle heart conditions. Researchers collect information about their medical care, health, and development during the first year of life. The study is also part of a national effort to help children's heart centers learn from one another and improve care for babies with single ventricle heart disease.
NCT02852031.who_might_this_be_for: Babies diagnosed before or shortly after birth with HLHS or another single ventricle heart condition may qualify if they are expected to have the Norwood procedure. The study lists no specific exclusion criteria. Families should ask their participating heart center whether their child can join the registry.
NCT02852031.why_might_this_matter: Care for babies with single ventricle heart disease is complex and can vary between heart centers. By collecting information from many families and hospitals, researchers can study which approaches are linked with better care and outcomes. The goal is to use what they learn to improve care for children with single ventricle heart disease.
NCT02852031.what_should_families_know: This is an observational registry, not a study of a new treatment. Joining does not assign a child to a medicine, device, or procedure. The study follows children for about 15 months and collects information about their care, health, and development. Many children's heart centers across the United States participate, along with sites in Canada and the United Kingdom. Families should ask their local study team what information will be collected and whether participation requires anything beyond their child's usual care.

NCT05206955.what_is_this_study_about: The TRIUMPH trial is testing whether tadalafil can improve blood flow and organ function in adults with Fontan circulation. Participants are randomly assigned to take either tadalafil or a placebo once a day for 52 weeks. A placebo looks like the study medicine but has no active drug. Neither participants nor the researchers know which treatment a person receives. Researchers will study how tadalafil affects blood flow through the lungs and the function of small blood vessels throughout the body.
NCT05206955.who_might_this_be_for: Adults age 18 or older who have had a Fontan procedure and are already having a cardiac catheterization for their medical care may qualify. Participants must also be able to exercise on a bike during testing. People taking certain medicines, including pulmonary vasodilators, nitrates, or alpha-blockers, cannot participate. People who are pregnant or breastfeeding also cannot participate. The study team will review all eligibility requirements.
NCT05206955.why_might_this_matter: People with Fontan circulation can develop problems with blood flow that may affect the heart and other organs. This study may help researchers learn whether tadalafil improves blood flow through the lungs and small blood vessels. Researchers will also look at exercise ability, kidney function, liver stiffness, and quality of life. Taking part may or may not directly improve a participant's health.
NCT05206955.what_should_families_know: Participation lasts about one year. Participants take tadalafil or a placebo every day, and the tadalafil dose is gradually increased during the first few weeks. Study testing includes exercise tests, heart imaging, kidney testing, and an MRI-based test that measures liver stiffness. The study also uses information from a cardiac catheterization that the participant is already having for medical reasons. Families should ask the study team how often they will need to travel to Mayo Clinic, which tests are part of the research, and what side effects are possible.

NCT07220226.what_is_this_study_about: This study is testing whether compression garments worn on the lower body can improve blood flow and heart function during exercise in adults with Fontan circulation. Participants exercise both with and without the garments while researchers measure how much blood returns to the heart and how much blood the heart pumps with each beat. Some participants will also wear the compression garments during the day for two weeks and then repeat the testing.
NCT07220226.who_might_this_be_for: Adults ages 18 through 45 with Fontan circulation who receive care at UT Southwestern may qualify. Some health problems may prevent someone from joining, including severe heart dysfunction or valve leakage, certain heart rhythm problems, a blood clot in the Fontan circulation, very low oxygen levels, or a recent unplanned heart-related hospital stay. People who are pregnant cannot participate. The study team will review all eligibility requirements.
NCT07220226.why_might_this_matter: People with Fontan circulation rely on blood flowing through the veins to reach the lungs without a ventricle pumping it there. Researchers want to learn whether compression garments can help more blood return to the heart during exercise and improve how much blood the heart pumps with each beat. The results could help researchers understand whether compression garments should be studied further as a way to support exercise in people with Fontan circulation.
NCT07220226.what_should_families_know: This study does not involve a medicine or surgery. Testing includes exercise while wearing and not wearing compression garments. Participants also have a leg vein ultrasound, heart MRI with exercise, echocardiogram, lung function testing, blood vessel testing, and a DEXA scan. Some participants will be asked to wear custom compression garments during waking hours for two weeks and then repeat the MRI and exercise testing. The study plans to enroll 20 people and also includes healthy volunteers for comparison.

NCT07087782.what_is_this_study_about: This study is testing whether a high-calorie formula called Fortini can help babies with single ventricle heart disease grow better between their first and second heart surgeries. Before leaving the hospital after Stage 1 surgery, babies are randomly assigned to receive either Fortini or the usual high-calorie nutrition used by their care team. Researchers will compare growth between the two groups and also look at feeding problems, hospital readmissions, and caregiver stress.
NCT07087782.who_might_this_be_for: Babies up to 6 months old with single ventricle heart disease who have had Stage 1 surgery, such as a Norwood, hybrid procedure, or BT shunt, may qualify. Babies must be medically ready to leave the hospital and may feed by mouth, NG tube, or G-tube. Some digestive conditions or a cow's milk protein allergy may prevent a baby from joining. Babies already taking part in another feeding or nutrition study also cannot participate. The study team will review all eligibility requirements.
NCT07087782.why_might_this_matter: Babies with single ventricle heart disease can have difficulty gaining enough weight between their first and second surgeries. Fortini provides more calories in a smaller amount of formula, which could be helpful for babies who have trouble taking larger feeding volumes. This study will help researchers learn whether Fortini supports better growth and how well babies tolerate it. Researchers will also study whether the feeding approach affects hospital readmissions and caregiver stress.
NCT07087782.what_should_families_know: This is a randomized study, so families cannot choose which feeding group their baby joins. Babies assigned to the Fortini group receive 30-calorie-per-ounce Fortini formula, while the other group receives standard high-calorie nutritional care. Babies are followed during the interstage period until their Stage 2 evaluation, usually about 4 to 6 months after hospital discharge. Researchers track weight gain, feeding tolerance, calorie intake, hospital readmissions, and caregiver-reported feeding stress. The study plans to enroll 100 babies.

NCT06324396.what_is_this_study_about: This study is looking at how the liver processes medicines in people with Fontan circulation. Participants receive one dose each of two medicines, sildenafil and pravastatin. Researchers then measure the amount of each medicine in the body. They want to learn whether liver congestion or scarring related to Fontan circulation changes how medicines are processed.
NCT06324396.who_might_this_be_for: People age 8 or older who have had the Fontan procedure may qualify. Participants must be able to swallow tablets and fast overnight before the study testing. People who have recently taken sildenafil or pravastatin, take certain medicines that interact with them, or have some kidney, intestinal, metabolic, or autoimmune conditions may not qualify. Pregnancy, a previous solid organ transplant, and some conditions that make MRI unsafe also prevent participation. The study team will review all eligibility requirements.
NCT06324396.why_might_this_matter: The liver can become congested and develop scarring after the Fontan procedure. These changes may also affect how the liver processes medicines, but researchers do not fully understand this yet. Learning more could eventually help doctors choose safer and more appropriate medication doses for people with Fontan circulation.
NCT06324396.what_should_families_know: This is a small Phase 1 study that plans to enroll 15 people. Participants receive only a single dose of sildenafil and a single dose of pravastatin for the research; this is not long-term treatment with either medicine. Participants must fast overnight before testing and be able to have an MRI. Families should ask the study team about the full testing schedule, including blood draws and imaging, how long the study visit will take, and the possible side effects of the medicines.

NCT06918795.what_is_this_study_about: This study is testing whether a personalized, home-based exercise program can help kids and teens with Fontan circulation become more active and physically fit. Participants are randomly assigned to either the digital exercise program or enhanced usual care. Everyone wears a physical activity tracker. Those in the exercise program also receive personalized aerobic and strength exercises through a digital platform for six months.
NCT06918795.who_might_this_be_for: Kids and teens ages 10 through 17 with Fontan circulation may qualify. Participants must be able to complete exercise testing and the other study activities. An exercise test at the beginning of the study is used to determine who can continue into the randomized trial. Some heart rhythm problems, severe exercise limitations, uncontrolled lymphatic problems, a pacemaker or implanted defibrillator, or having had or being considered for a heart transplant may prevent someone from joining. The study team will review all eligibility requirements.
NCT06918795.why_might_this_matter: Kids and teens with Fontan circulation can have lower exercise ability and may be less physically active than their peers. This study will help researchers learn whether a personalized exercise program that can be done at home improves physical activity, fitness, muscle strength, and quality of life. It may also help researchers understand which young people benefit most from this type of program.
NCT06918795.what_should_families_know: Participation lasts about one year. Everyone wears a physical activity tracker and completes testing at the beginning of the study and again at 6 and 12 months. Participants assigned to the exercise program complete personalized aerobic and strength exercises for six months and meet regularly with an exercise physiologist, starting weekly and becoming less frequent over time. Participants assigned to enhanced usual care continue their usual care and use the activity tracker but do not receive the digital exercise program. Families should ask the study team what the testing visits involve, how much time the home exercises require, and what equipment or technology is needed.

NCT06469918.what_is_this_study_about: The Co-Op @ HeartWorks is a long-term registry for people and families affected by congenital heart disease. Members share information about their medical journey to help researchers better understand the needs of the congenital heart disease community. The Co-Op also aims to give members a role in shaping future research and the design of clinical trials.
NCT06469918.who_might_this_be_for: Adults with congenital heart disease may join for themselves. Parents or caregivers may join on behalf of a child with congenital heart disease. An authorized family member may also participate on behalf of someone with congenital heart disease who has died. The registry includes many types of congenital heart disease, not only single ventricle heart disease.
NCT06469918.why_might_this_matter: Information collected from many people with congenital heart disease may help researchers identify important questions and plan future studies. The Co-Op is also designed to include patients and families in decisions about future research. Researchers hope this partnership will lead to studies that better reflect the needs and priorities of people affected by congenital heart disease.
NCT06469918.what_should_families_know: This is an observational registry, not a study of a medicine, device, or procedure. Joining does not assign a participant to a treatment. The registry is designed for long-term participation, with follow-up planned for up to 25 years. Information collected through the registry may also be used to help plan and recruit for future clinical trials. Families should ask what medical information will be collected, how often they will be asked to provide updates, how their information may be used or shared, and how members can participate in shaping future research.

NCT07073612.what_is_this_study_about: This study is looking at what happens after a narrowed Fontan conduit is opened with a stent. Researchers want to learn whether exercise ability and liver stiffness change after the procedure. Participants complete exercise testing and liver stiffness scans before and after their Fontan stent placement.
NCT07073612.who_might_this_be_for: People ages 12 through 21 with single ventricle heart disease and an extracardiac Fontan may qualify if they are already scheduled for a cardiac catheterization and their care team expects to place a stent for narrowing of the Fontan conduit. Participants must weigh at least 50 kg and be able to complete an exercise test. Some heart rhythm problems, a pacemaker, significant heart valve leakage, or decreased heart function may prevent someone from joining. The study team will review all eligibility requirements.
NCT07073612.why_might_this_matter: Narrowing of the Fontan conduit can affect blood flow through the Fontan circulation. Researchers want to learn whether opening the narrowed area with a stent is followed by improvements in exercise ability or changes in liver stiffness. The results may help researchers better understand the effects of Fontan conduit stenting beyond simply opening the narrowed blood vessel.
NCT07073612.what_should_families_know: The decision to have a Fontan stent placed is made as part of the participant's medical care, not by this study. Research testing includes two cardiopulmonary exercise tests and three liver stiffness scans. Testing begins before the cardiac catheterization and continues for several months afterward. Each exercise test takes about one hour, while each liver stiffness scan takes about 20 minutes. The study plans to enroll 20 participants.

NCT06150950.what_is_this_study_about: This study is testing whether cardiac rehabilitation can help adults who are experiencing problems with their Fontan circulation. Participants are randomly assigned to either a 12-week cardiac rehabilitation program or usual care. Researchers will compare daily activity, exercise ability, physical strength and frailty, and quality of life between the two groups.
NCT06150950.who_might_this_be_for: Adults age 18 or older who have had a Fontan procedure and have signs of Fontan failure may qualify. These signs can include decreased heart function, protein-losing enteropathy, plastic bronchitis, needing certain diuretic medicines, or significantly reduced exercise ability. Some heart rhythm problems, very low oxygen levels, a recent Fontan-related procedure, or already participating in cardiac rehabilitation may prevent someone from joining. The study team will review all eligibility requirements.
NCT06150950.why_might_this_matter: People experiencing Fontan failure can have difficulty exercising and may become less physically active or physically frail. Cardiac rehabilitation combines supervised, personalized exercise with support to help people safely increase activity. This study will help researchers learn whether cardiac rehabilitation improves activity, exercise ability, physical function, and quality of life for adults with Fontan failure.
NCT06150950.what_should_families_know: Participants are randomly assigned to cardiac rehabilitation or usual care. Everyone receives a Fitbit to track daily activity. The cardiac rehabilitation program includes three sessions each week for 12 weeks. At Vanderbilt, the program is completely virtual. Stanford participants may take part in person, virtually, or through a combination of the two. Participants assigned to usual care do not begin cardiac rehabilitation during the study comparison period. Study testing includes cardiopulmonary exercise testing, walking and strength tests, body composition measurements, and questionnaires about physical activity, mood, nutrition, and quality of life.

NCT05213598.what_is_this_study_about: This study is trying to understand how Fontan circulation affects the liver over time. Researchers are studying why long-term blood congestion can lead to liver scarring and cirrhosis. They are also looking for signs in blood, liver tissue, genes, and other samples that could help doctors measure the severity of Fontan-associated liver disease and follow it over time.
NCT05213598.who_might_this_be_for: Adults age 18 or older who have had a Fontan procedure and are at risk for Fontan-associated liver disease may qualify. Participants must also have previously taken part in a specific NIH liver study and have had a cardiac catheterization or liver biopsy within the past 10 years. Other types of liver disease, some serious medical conditions, pregnancy, or a severe allergy to contrast may prevent someone from joining. The study team will review all eligibility requirements.
NCT05213598.why_might_this_matter: Liver disease is an important long-term complication of Fontan circulation, but researchers still do not fully understand why some people develop more severe liver scarring than others. This study may help identify better ways to measure and monitor Fontan-associated liver disease. Researchers also hope what they learn could eventually help with decisions about when a heart or combined heart-liver transplant should be considered.
NCT05213598.what_should_families_know: This is an observational research study and does not test a treatment. Participation includes several visits and a 3-day hospital stay. Testing includes blood and urine tests, heart testing, liver ultrasound and FibroScan, MRI with contrast, stool collection, questionnaires, an upper endoscopy, and a liver biopsy. Before the biopsy, a catheter is placed through a vein in the neck to measure pressures in the liver. The study record states that there is no direct benefit from participation. Families should ask the study team which procedures are being done only for research, what risks they involve, and whether travel or other costs are covered.

NCT05262907.what_is_this_study_about: This study is testing a new way to measure heart size and function in people with functional single ventricle heart disease. The technique, called Ventripoint 3D echocardiography, uses ultrasound to create three-dimensional measurements of the heart. Researchers will compare these measurements with standard heart imaging, including echocardiograms and cardiac MRI.
NCT05262907.who_might_this_be_for: Children and adults with functional single ventricle heart disease may qualify, regardless of their age or stage of surgical treatment. Participants must have had or be having an echocardiogram or cardiac MRI ordered as part of their medical care. People following a pathway to convert from single ventricle to two-ventricle circulation are not eligible. The study team will review all eligibility requirements.
NCT05262907.why_might_this_matter: Measuring heart size and function can be difficult in people with single ventricle heart disease because their hearts may have shapes that are different from a typical heart. Researchers want to learn whether Ventripoint 3D echocardiography can provide accurate measurements in these patients. If it works well, this technology could provide another way to evaluate heart function in people with single ventricle heart disease.
NCT05262907.what_should_families_know: The Ventripoint 3D echocardiogram is a noninvasive ultrasound of the heart. This study does not test a medicine or treatment. Participants are already having or have previously had a standard echocardiogram or cardiac MRI for their medical care, and researchers compare those images with the Ventripoint measurements. The study measurements are collected on a single day and the study plans to enroll 100 participants.

NCT06434207.what_is_this_study_about: This study is looking at why newborns with severe congenital heart disease may be at higher risk of developing blood clots around the time of heart surgery. Researchers will study patterns in blood samples collected before and after surgery to better understand how the body's clotting system changes.
NCT06434207.who_might_this_be_for: Newborns with severe congenital heart disease who have heart surgery at Boston Children's Hospital during their first week of life may qualify. The study includes babies with different types of severe congenital heart disease, not only single ventricle heart disease. The study record lists no additional exclusion criteria.
NCT06434207.why_might_this_matter: Blood clots can be a serious complication for newborns with congenital heart disease after heart surgery. Researchers do not yet fully understand the biological changes that may make some babies more likely to develop them. Learning more about these changes could help researchers identify better ways to understand and eventually reduce the risk of blood clots.
NCT06434207.what_should_families_know: This is an observational study and does not test a medicine or treatment. Researchers use leftover blood from routine clinical blood samples that would otherwise be discarded. One sample is collected from blood drawn before surgery and another from blood drawn after surgery, so the study record does not describe additional blood draws for the research. The samples are used to study genetic material called microRNA and other processes related to inflammation and blood clotting. The study plans to enroll 10 newborns.

NCT05386173.what_is_this_study_about: This study is looking at babies diagnosed before birth with severe narrowing of the aortic valve that may lead to hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS). Researchers are comparing babies who have fetal aortic valvuloplasty, a procedure that uses a balloon to open the narrowed valve before birth, with babies who do not have the procedure. They want to learn whether left-heart growth and outcomes after birth differ between the two groups.
NCT05386173.who_might_this_be_for: This study may include pregnancies in which the fetus has severe aortic valve narrowing and specific findings on fetal echocardiograms between 23 and 31 weeks of pregnancy. The findings must suggest that the left side of the heart is at risk of becoming too small to support circulation after birth. The study has detailed heart measurements and other eligibility requirements that the fetal cardiology team will review.
NCT05386173.why_might_this_matter: In some fetuses, severe narrowing of the aortic valve can prevent the left side of the heart from growing normally and may lead to HLHS. Fetal aortic valvuloplasty is performed at some heart centers in an effort to change this course, but researchers do not yet know how much it improves long-term outcomes. This study will compare outcomes to better understand the possible benefits and risks of the procedure.
NCT05386173.what_should_families_know: This is an observational study. The decision about whether to attempt fetal aortic valvuloplasty is made separately from the research, and joining the study does not change the care or testing that the mother or baby receives. Researchers collect clinical information and heart imaging from pregnancies in which the procedure is performed and from a comparison group in which it is not. The study follows children after birth and looks at survival without heart transplantation, whether a two-ventricle circulation is possible, heart growth, and possible risks of the fetal procedure, including fetal death, premature delivery, and serious complications for the mother.

NCT07686341.what_is_this_study_about: This study is testing a new pulse oximeter designed to measure a baby's oxygen level from the abdomen instead of a finger or other limb. Researchers will compare readings from the new device with standard pulse oximeter readings and oxygen measurements from arterial blood. They want to learn whether the abdominal device provides accurate readings while reducing errors caused by movement.
NCT07686341.who_might_this_be_for: Babies younger than 1 year who weigh more than 2 kg may qualify. For hospitalized participants, babies must already be in an intensive care unit, have an arterial line placed for their medical care, and be receiving continuous oxygen monitoring. Babies with an open chest, certain skin problems where the sensor would be placed, or sensitivity to the device materials may not qualify. The study team will review all eligibility requirements.
NCT07686341.why_might_this_matter: Pulse oximeters can sometimes give inaccurate readings, especially when babies move. Skin tone may also affect the accuracy of some pulse oximeters. Researchers are developing this abdominal monitor to try to provide more reliable oxygen readings while accounting for movement and differences in skin tone. More accurate monitoring could eventually help caregivers recognize low oxygen levels more reliably.
NCT07686341.what_should_families_know: This is an observational study and does not test a medicine or treatment. The new pulse oximeter is placed against the baby's abdomen and clips onto the diaper or clothing. It is removed during diaper changes. The baby's usual clinical monitoring continues, and researchers compare the new device's readings with information already being collected during the baby's care. Participation lasts up to 3 days, with no additional study visits. The study plans to enroll 100 babies.

NCT07532369.what_is_this_study_about: This study is looking at the safety and effectiveness of a device called the Occlutech Atrial Flow Regulator in people with a failing Fontan circulation. The device is designed to create or adjust an opening, called a fenestration, that allows blood to flow between parts of the circulation. Researchers are reviewing information from patients who have already had placement of this device attempted through the FDA Expanded Access Program.
NCT07532369.who_might_this_be_for: This study includes children and adults with a failing Fontan circulation who have already had an Occlutech Atrial Flow Regulator procedure attempted or completed through the FDA Expanded Access Program. It is not enrolling people to receive the device as part of this research study.
NCT07532369.why_might_this_matter: Creating or changing the size of a Fontan fenestration may help lower high pressure in the veins for some people with a failing Fontan circulation. Researchers want to learn more about the safety of the Occlutech Atrial Flow Regulator and whether the opening created with the device remains open over time. The results may help researchers better understand how the device performs in people with Fontan failure.
NCT07532369.what_should_families_know: This is a retrospective observational study. Researchers use medical information that was already collected during the care of patients who previously had the device procedure attempted. No new procedures or treatments are given as part of this study. Researchers will look for serious problems related to the device or procedure and will evaluate whether blood is still flowing through the opening one year after the procedure. The study plans to include about 25 patients.

NCT06175104.what_is_this_study_about: This study is testing a support program called HeartGPS for parents who learn during pregnancy that their baby has single ventricle heart disease. Participants are randomly assigned to receive either usual fetal cardiac care or usual care plus HeartGPS. HeartGPS includes eight sessions with a psychologist, educational resources, and a personalized care plan. Researchers want to learn whether the program improves parent emotional wellbeing and may also affect bonding, infant brain development, and development during the baby's first year.
NCT06175104.who_might_this_be_for: Pregnant adults whose baby is diagnosed with single ventricle heart disease between 16 and 30 weeks of pregnancy may qualify. The pregnancy must involve one baby, and the parent must be planning to continue the pregnancy and be able to complete study activities in English. Certain fetal health conditions and some untreated mental health or substance use conditions may prevent participation. The study team will review all eligibility requirements.
NCT06175104.why_might_this_matter: Learning during pregnancy that a baby has single ventricle heart disease can be stressful and overwhelming. HeartGPS is designed to help parents cope with the diagnosis, support their emotional wellbeing, and build a connection with their baby. This study will help researchers learn whether providing this type of support during pregnancy and after birth reduces anxiety, depression, and traumatic stress and whether it may also support parent-infant relationships and infant development.
NCT06175104.what_should_families_know: Participants are randomly assigned to HeartGPS plus usual fetal cardiac care or to usual care alone. HeartGPS sessions can be completed in person or by telehealth. The study follows parents and babies through about the baby's first year and includes questionnaires and developmental assessments. Research also includes fetal and infant MRI scans and collection of samples such as blood, saliva, and placental tissue. Families should ask the study team about the schedule for the eight HeartGPS sessions and the time and travel required for imaging, sample collection, and follow-up assessments.

NCT06932081.what_is_this_study_about: This international registry is studying the use of medicines called SGLT2 inhibitors in adults with congenital heart disease. Researchers are collecting information from people who have already been prescribed one of these medicines as part of their medical care. They want to learn how SGLT2 inhibitors are being used, how well people tolerate them, and whether changes in heart failure-related health are seen after treatment begins.
NCT06932081.who_might_this_be_for: Adults age 18 or older with congenital heart disease who are taking or have previously taken an SGLT2 inhibitor may qualify. The registry includes many types of congenital heart disease, including people with Fontan circulation and other forms of single ventricle heart disease. The decision to prescribe an SGLT2 inhibitor is made as part of the person's medical care, not by this study.
NCT06932081.why_might_this_matter: SGLT2 inhibitors are used to treat heart failure in many adults, but there is less information about their use in people with congenital heart disease. This registry will help researchers learn more about their safety, side effects, and possible benefits in this population. Researchers will also look at people with Fontan and other single ventricle circulations to better understand how these medicines are being used for their heart failure.
NCT06932081.what_should_families_know: This is an observational registry and does not assign participants to take an SGLT2 inhibitor or change their treatment. Researchers collect information already available from routine medical care, including information from before and after the medicine was started. They will look at side effects, reasons for stopping treatment, hospital visits, heart and kidney measurements, heart imaging, and exercise testing when those results are available. The registry plans to include about 400 adults with different types of congenital heart disease.
